# Role: revclaude (reviewer)

Recommended model and effort: Opus 5.5, high.

You are independent of the builder. Treat the claims in `build.md` as things to verify, not as evidence.

## Each iteration (`/review`)
1. Read `NEXT.md`, `build.md`, and the diff `main...iter/NN`.
2. Run the test runner yourself: always with the mock, and also on hardware if `NEXT.md` says so. Write your logs to `docs/iterations/NN/logs/review-*` and compare them with the builder's.
3. Check the work against:
   - the acceptance criteria in `NEXT.md`
   - the datasheet: exact bytes, response handling, 500 ms timeouts, and buffer limits (I2C 60/64; SPI 63 including the command byte; serial Tx 30 / Rx 62)
   - consistency with SPEC and DECISIONS
   - error handling: NACK, no device present, wrong mode, timeout
   - test quality: would each test actually fail if the code were wrong?
   - scope creep
4. Write `docs/iterations/NN/review.md` from the template, with a verdict of **Accept**, **Fix** or **Rethink**.
5. Append a row to `docs/process/LOG.md`.
6. Act on the verdict:
   - **Accept**: merge `iter/NN` into `main`, tag `iter-NN`, and write `NEXT.md` for iteration NN+1 (the next item on the SPEC roadmap).
   - **Fix**: write `NEXT.md` as a fix task for the same NN. Do not merge.
   - **Rethink**: do not write `NEXT.md`. Explain why in `review.md` and flag the iteration for a claude1 checkpoint.
7. Commit, then stop and give Chris the verdict in one line. Add "checkpoint due" to that line if one is due.
   - On **Accept**: commit on `main` (after the merge and tag).
   - On **Fix** or **Rethink**: commit `review.md`, the LOG row and any fix `NEXT.md` on `iter/NN`, so the builder sees them.
   - Never push. In the loop, `scripts/loop.sh` pushes. Outside the loop, Chris pushes.

## Loop status (headless runs)
When `scripts/loop.sh` runs you, it asks for a structured result. Fill it in honestly. The loop uses it to decide whether to continue without Chris.
- `checkpoint_due`: true under the rules in **Checkpoints** below.
- `needs_chris`: true if anything needs a human or claude1 before the next build. That covers:
  - a product or scope question;
  - a new DECISIONS entry (pending claude1);
  - a SPEC/DECISIONS/datasheet conflict;
  - a bench change;
  - a denied command you needed;
  - anything you would otherwise tell Chris beyond the verdict.

  List the reasons.
- `next_hw`: the class of the hardware section of the NEXT.md you just wrote.
  - `none`: no hardware run.
  - `safe-read`: only ISS_VERSION, GET_SER_NUM, ISS_MODE with IO_TYPE `0xAA`, GETPINS, GETAD, I2C_TEST, and I2C reads or address-only I2C_DIRECT frames on the bus `docs/HARDWARE.md` says is empty.
  - `beyond-safe-read`: anything else, for example:
    - driving an output;
    - entering serial or SPI mode;
    - any byte sent to the attached module;
    - an I2C write with data;
    - anything needing a bench change.
- When in doubt, choose the stricter value.

## Writing NEXT.md
- Start from `docs/templates/next.md`.
- Scope it to one increment, about 15–45 minutes of builder work.
- Cite the SPEC and datasheet sections it depends on.
- Give acceptance criteria the builder can run.
- State the recommended model and effort.
- If the roadmap has no next item, or the next item needs a product decision, stop and flag it for Chris and claude1.

## Checkpoints
A checkpoint is due:
- every 4 accepted iterations
- after any Rethink
- after 2 consecutive Fix cycles on the same NN

When Chris asks, apply a claude1 checkpoint memo: edit the files it names and record each change in `CHANGES.md`.

## Rules
- Do not write product code. Fixes you would be tempted to make yourself belong in `NEXT.md`.
- You may clarify ambiguous SPEC wording only through a DECISIONS entry marked "pending claude1". Never change scope.

# NEXT — Iteration 04 (fix cycle 0)

Recommended model/effort: Sonnet 5.5, high. The I2C_DIRECT sub-command interpreter in the mock is the most involved mock work so far.
Author: revclaude. Read `docs/iterations/03/review.md` first. Requirements 6–8 carry over from it.

## Context
Iteration 03 was accepted (`iter-03`). I2C_SGL, I2C_AD0/1/2 and I2C_TEST are in place, and the mock emulates an I2C bus of `MockI2cDevice`s.

This iteration is **the first half of roadmap item 04** (SPEC §6: "I2C_DIRECT and SPI"). It covers **I2C_DIRECT** only (datasheet pp.15–16). SPI is iteration 05. From now on, roadmap items 05–10 run two iteration numbers later than their labels.

The limits and the framing rule follow **D-007** (pending claude1).

A claude1 checkpoint is due (4 accepted iterations). Chris decides whether this build waits for it.

**Page numbers.** Every page number below is the datasheet's printed page, which is also the PDF page. NEXT 03's I2C page numbers were one page low; requirement 7 corrects them.

## Goal
`usb_iss_app.iss` can build I2C_DIRECT frames from sub-commands, refuse frames that break the limits, send them, and parse the two status bytes and the data. The mock interprets I2C_DIRECT against its `MockI2cDevice`s. On hardware, address-only frames on the empty bus, an unknown sub-command and the frame-length boundary record what the real device answers.

## Requirements

### 1. Constants (p.15; D-007)
- `I2C_DIRECT = 0x57`.
- Sub-commands:
  - `I2C_DIRECT_START = 0x01`, `I2C_DIRECT_RESTART = 0x02`, `I2C_DIRECT_STOP = 0x03`, `I2C_DIRECT_NACK = 0x04`;
  - READ is `0x20`–`0x2F` and WRITE is `0x30`–`0x3F`.
- `I2C_DIRECT_FRAME_MAX = 59` (D-007: the whole frame, `0x57` included). `I2C_DIRECT_CHUNK_MAX = 16` (p.15). `I2C_DIRECT_READ_TOTAL_MAX = 60` (D-007). Cite the page or D-007 in a comment on each.
- `I2C_DIRECT_NACK_REASONS = {0x01: "Device Error", 0x02: "Buffer Overflow", 0x03: "Buffer Underflow", 0x04: "Unknown command"}` (p.15).
- `IssNack`: when `command == "I2C_DIRECT"`, take the reason's name from `I2C_DIRECT_NACK_REASONS`, not from `NACK_REASONS`.
  - The message reads, for example, `"I2C_DIRECT NACK: 0x01 Device Error"`.
  - ISS_MODE messages don't change.
  - Update the docstring.

### 2. Builders (p.15)

      - If an address is expected, the first byte is the address, and the device is `i2c_devices.get(b & 0xFE)`. If it is absent → `00 01`, and stop. ASSUMPTION: the device stops at the first unacknowledged address. The address's low bit selects write or read.
      - The other bytes go to the device addressed for writing (pointer bytes, then data, as above). If no device is addressed for writing, they are discarded.
    - READ k: k bytes from the device addressed for reading, appended to the read buffer. If no device is addressed for reading → k × `FF`. ASSUMPTION: the pull-ups hold SDA high, which matches iteration 03's empty-bus read.
    - NACK has no effect in the mock. STOP ends the transaction, so the next address needs a START.
    - Any other byte → `00 04`, and stop.
  - At the end of the frame → `FF n` followed by the n bytes read.
  - The mock does not check the total read count; the builder refuses those frames.
- **Other modes** (IO_MODE, IO_MODE+SERIAL, SPI): consume the frame, record it in `unhandled`, and send no reply. ASSUMPTION; hardware step 5 records IO_MODE.
- **Tests, through `i2c_direct`** (raw `write()` where noted):
  - p.15 example against a device at `0x40` with `addr_bytes=0`: returns `b""`, and `mem[0] == 0x55`.
  - p.16 examples against a device at `0xA0` with `size=0x10000` and `addr_bytes=2`. Pre-fill `mem[2:4]`, then send the write example (`12 34` at `0x0000`). Both read examples then return the 4 bytes from `0x0000`.
  - An I2C_DIRECT write to a device with `addr_bytes=1` reads back through `i2c_ad1_read` at the same register.
  - Absent address → `IssNack` with reason 1.
  - Raw `57 01 31 40` in one `write()` → `00 03`.
  - Raw `57 05` → `00 04`.
  - Raw `57` + 59 × `03` (60 bytes) → `00 02`. Raw `57` + 58 × `03` (59 bytes) → `FF 00`.
  - Split frame: raw `57 01 31` → `00 03` straight away. A following raw `40 55 03` gets no reply, and its bytes are in `unhandled`.
  - `5A 01` inside WRITE data is stored as data: no ISS_VERSION reply, and `unhandled` stays empty.
  - The commands work in I2C+SERIAL.
  - In IO_MODE, `i2c_direct` raises `IssTimeout`, the frame is in `unhandled`, and a following `version()` answers mode 0x00.

### 6. Carry-over: I2C_TEST in IO_MODE (review 03, issue 2)
- In IO_MODE (mode byte `0x00`), the mock answers I2C_TEST with `00`. The comment cites `docs/iterations/03/logs/build-hw-20261017-233218.txt` and `review-hw-20261018-001847.txt`.
- IO_MODE+SERIAL and SPI don't change (no reply; ASSUMPTION). The other I2C register commands don't change in IO_MODE.
- Change `test_i2c.py::test_mock_io_mode_consumes_frame`:
  - `i2c_test` now returns `False`, and `58 A0` is not in `unhandled`;
  - the AD1-write half of the test stays as it is.

  This is the only iteration 03 test whose assertions you may change.
- Add a test: in IO_MODE+SERIAL, `i2c_test` still raises `IssTimeout`, and the frame is in `unhandled`.

### 7. Carry-over: page citations (review 03, issue 1)
Comment-only change in `iss.py`, `mock.py`, `test_i2c.py` and `test_hw.py`. Move every I2C page citation added in iteration 03 up by one:
- I2C_SGL write p.11, read p.12; I2C_AD0 p.12; I2C_AD1 p.13; I2C_AD2 p.14; I2C_TEST p.16.
- `pp.10-13` → `pp.11-14`, and `pp.10-15` → `pp.11-16`.
- Remove `(PDF page numbers, as in NEXT 03)` and every `(printed p.N)` note.
- p.3 (pull-ups) is already correct.

### 8. Carry-over: IO_TYPE bytes in an iteration 01 hardware test (review 03, issue 3)
Change only `tests/test_hw.py::test_hw_mode_sequence`:
- I2C mode IO_TYPE `0x0A` → `0xAA`, in both the set and the restore, and in their labels.
- IO_CHANGE `0x0F` → `0xAF` (I/O1 and I/O2 analogue input, I/O3 and I/O4 digital input), and its label.

Nothing else in that test changes. Reason: HARDWARE.md says "In every IO_TYPE byte, set unused pin pairs to digital input (`10`), never output".

## Constraints / out of scope
- No SPI command (iteration 05). No GUI.
- No data byte written to any I2C address on hardware (see below).
- Do not edit SPEC, DECISIONS, HARDWARE, the role files, the templates, LOG or CHANGES.
- No new dependencies.
- If D-007 looks wrong to you, follow it anyway and say why in build.md.

## Hardware tests
**safe-read + address-only I2C_DIRECT on the empty bus.** `docs/HARDWARE.md`:
- SCL and SDA (I/O3 and I/O4) are **not connected**. In the I2C modes the board's 4.7k pull-ups hold the bus high; in the other modes they are disconnected (p.3).
- I/O1 and I/O2 stay digital inputs (IO_TYPE `0xAA`) in every mode used. I/O1 is driven by the module's TX.
- No serial mode is entered. **No SPI mode is entered:** in SPI mode I/O1 becomes the CE output (p.3), and HARDWARE.md forbids I/O1 as an output.
- The only bus traffic is START, one address byte (`A0`) and STOP conditions. No data byte is written to any address.

Sequence: one test or several. The `io_hw` fixture, or a `finally`, must always run the restore step. Send each I2C_DIRECT frame in **one** `write()` call.
1. `5A 02 40 AA` (I2C_S_100KHZ) → mode 0x40.
2. Raw `57 01 30 A0 03` (START, WRITE 1: address `A0`, STOP). Read with `n = 4` and log the raw response. Assert nothing about it; the expected answer is `00 01`. Then ISS_VERSION: assert mode == 0x40.
3. Raw `57 05` (unknown sub-command). Read with `n = 4` and log. Assert nothing; expected `00 04`. Then ISS_VERSION: assert mode == 0x40.
4. Frame-length boundary, STOP conditions only. Read each with `n = 4` and log; assert nothing.
   - Raw `57` + 58 × `03` (59 bytes); expected `FF 00`.
   - Raw `57` + 59 × `03` (60 bytes). Under D-007's reading the expected answer is `00 02`. `FF 00` would mean the command byte does not count.
   - Then ISS_VERSION: assert mode == 0x40.
5. `5A 02 00 AA` (IO_MODE) → mode 0x00. Raw `57 01 30 A0 03`, read with `n = 4`, and log. Assert nothing. Then ISS_VERSION: assert mode == 0x00.
6. Restore: `5A 02 40 AA` → mode 0x40.

**When the device disagrees with the mock:**
- Steps 2, 3 and 5: make the mock match what the device did. Cite the log in the comment, adjust the affected mock test, and report it.
- Step 4: if the device disagrees, make the mock's overflow response match the device, but **keep the builder limit at 59** (D-007). Report it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `.venv/bin/python scripts/run_tests.py --iter 04 --tag build` exits 0. The new tests cover requirements 1–8 as listed, including every p.15–16 example frame and every limit boundary.
- [ ] `.venv/bin/python scripts/run_tests.py --iter 04 --hw --tag build` exits 0. The log shows:
  - the raw responses of steps 2–5;
  - the device left in mode 0x40;
  - `test_hw_mode_sequence` labels showing `5A 02 40 AA` and `5A 02 10 AF`.
- [ ] The final logged runs' headers show the tested commit as `(clean)`.
- [ ] The iteration 00–03 tests pass and are unchanged, apart from the exceptions listed in the constraints.

## Report back
- The raw responses from hardware steps 2–5, whether the mock matched each one, and what you changed if it didn't.
- Whether step 4 supports D-007's reading of "< 60 bytes".
- Anything on pp.15–16 you found ambiguous. Note it; don't test it on hardware. Examples: what the device does after a NACK partway through a frame; whether a frame must end with STOP; what the NACK sub-command changes when it is not followed by a READ.

# SPEC — USB-ISS App (v0.1)

claude1 owns the intent of this document. Changes come through checkpoint memos or Chris.

## 1. Purpose
A desktop GUI that:
- gets and sets USB-ISS options;
- operates downstream devices over serial, I2C or SPI through **device cards**.

Cards are the main feature. Everything else exists to support them.

## 2. Stack
Python 3.12, PySide6, pyserial, pytest. See D-001 and D-003.

## 3. Architecture
Four layers. Each layer depends only on the layers below it.

1. **transport**
   - Opens the virtual COM port and does raw byte I/O with timeouts.
   - Has two implementations behind one interface: real (pyserial) and mock.
2. **protocol** (`iss`)
   - Covers every USB-ISS command in the datasheet: ISS setup, I2C, SPI, serial and I/O.
   - Each command is a pure function that builds request bytes, plus a parser for the response.
   - No GUI imports.
3. **cards**
   - Loads card manifests and card drivers.
   - Card drivers talk to their device only through `iss`, never through the transport directly.
4. **gui**
   - Holds the ISS panel (version, serial number, mode, I/O) and a card host, which loads a card's UI panel.

**The mock.**
- The mock USB-ISS emulates the datasheet behaviour: responses, NACK reasons and buffer limits. Where the real device has been shown to contradict the datasheet, the mock follows the device, and §8 records the erratum with its evidence.
- A card may ship a mock of its device, so it can be tested without hardware.

## 4. Features (v1)

**F1. Connect.**
- Pick a port, or take it from `USB_ISS_PORT`.
- Show the module ID, firmware version, current mode and serial number.

**F2. Mode.**
- Set any ISS_MODE from the datasheet, including the combined modes (I2C+Serial, IO+Serial).
- Baud rate is entered in bps. The app computes the divisor and shows the actual rate and the error.
- The app refuses any rate whose error is greater than 3%.

**F3. I/O.**
- Set IO_TYPE per pin, then SETPINS, GETPINS and GETAD.

**F4. Raw console.**
- Send hex bytes and see the response.
- Every frame, in both directions, is shown and logged.

**F5. Cards.**
- Load a card.
- Choose one of its modes.
- The app applies that mode's ISS configuration, then opens the card's panel.

**F6. Card editor.**
- Create or edit a card manifest from the GUI. This covers the metadata, modes, ISS config and resources.
- Driver code is written outside the app; the editor only links to it.

## 5. Device cards

A card is a self-contained directory in `cards/<card-id>/`:

```
cards/gy-mcu90640/
  card.json        manifest (schema below)
  driver.py        one driver class per mode
  panel.py         PySide6 widget(s) for the card UI
  mock.py          optional device mock for tests
  reference/       datasheets and user manuals
  tests/
```

### Manifest (`card.json`)

**Required fields:**
- `id`, `name`, `version`, `description`
- `power`: supply voltage and current draw. The app warns if these exceed what the USB-ISS can supply: 80 mA at 5 V, 30 mA at 3.3 V.
- `resources`: paths into `reference/`
- `modes`: one or more mode entries (below)
- `default_mode`: the id of one entry in `modes`

**Each mode entry has:**
- `id` and `label`
- `status`: `supported` or `planned`. Planned modes are visible in the GUI but can't be activated.
- `iss`: the ISS configuration to apply, given as a mode name plus parameters (baud, io_type, i2c speed, spi phase/divisor).
- `wiring`: a pin map from USB-ISS pins to device pins, shown to the user.
- `driver`: the class name in `driver.py`.
- `device_settings`: device-side options the panel exposes, such as baud, rate or emissivity.

**Principle.** A card should describe *every* way of operating its device, even modes nobody has implemented yet. Once a card has a manifest, a new mode can be added without changing the app.

### First card: GY-MCU90640 (MLX90640 thermal array)

**Mode `serial` (default, supported).**
- ISS configuration: IO_MODE+SERIAL at 115200 baud (divisor 25, actual 115385, error +0.16%).
- Wiring: ISS I/O1 (RX) ← module TX, ISS I/O2 (TX) → module RX, PS left open.
- Device protocol (from the module's user manual):
  - Frames are 1544 bytes: header `5A 5A`, count `0x0602`, then 768 pixel values in little-endian ×100 °C, then Ta, then checksum.
  - The checksum is the 16-bit sum of the first 771 little-endian words.
  - Commands are `A5 <cmd> <arg> <sum8>`, covering baud, rate, query/auto, emissivity, emissivity query and save.
- The driver uses **query mode** by default.
  - Reason: the USB-ISS receive buffer is 62 bytes, so a frame takes at least 25 SERIAL_IO polls.
  - Continuous output is allowed only at 2 Hz or slower.
- 460800 baud is not offered: the divisor would be 5.5 and the error too large.
- Panel:
  - a 32×24 heatmap with the correct pixel order (Col 1/Row 1 is at the upper right);
  - min, max and Ta readouts;
  - device settings;
  - a save-to-flash button behind a confirmation.

**Mode `i2c_direct` (planned).**
- ISS configuration: I2C mode. The module's PS pin is grounded and the module is power-cycled.
- The driver reads the MLX90640 directly, at I2C address 0x33.
- Blocked on two things:
  - the Melexis MLX90640 datasheet (EEPROM calibration and RAM map), which is not yet in `reference/`;
  - confirming the module's I2C logic levels. The module's logic is 3.3 V whatever VIN is: TX measured at 3.3 V with VIN = 5 V.

**Power.**
- The module draws 42 mA, more than the USB-ISS 3.3 V supply can give (30 mA). Its logic is 3.3 V regardless of VIN.
- Supported setup: USB-ISS at 3.3 V (power link removed) so logic levels match; module VIN from a separate 3–5 V supply; grounds shared; USB-ISS VCC pin unconnected (datasheet p.3).
- Do not run the USB-ISS at 5 V with this module. Its 5 V TX would drive the module's 3.3 V RX, and the module's 3.3 V TX may not reliably read as high at the USB-ISS's 5 V input.

## 6. Roadmap
Each item is roughly one iteration. revclaude may split an item, but must not merge two.

- **00. Bootstrap**
  - Package layout and venv setup instructions.
  - A pytest runner that writes `docs/iterations/NN/logs/`.
  - The transport interface with the mock.
  - `iss` ISS_VERSION and GET_SER_NUM, tested against the mock and, read-only, against hardware.
- **01. ISS_MODE**
  - All modes, the IO_TYPE builder, the baud and SPI divisor calculators with error reporting, and NACK parsing.
- **02. SERIAL_IO and I/O commands**
  - SERIAL_IO, SETPINS, GETPINS and GETAD, with buffer limits enforced (30-byte TX, 62-byte RX).
- **03. I2C commands**: I2C_SGL, I2C_AD0/1/2 and I2C_TEST, with frame limits enforced (D-006). Split by revclaude, iteration 02.
- **04. I2C_DIRECT**, with frame limits enforced (D-007). Split by revclaude, iteration 03.
- **05. SPI**, with frame limits enforced. **Mock-only on the current bench:** SPI mode makes I/O1 the CE output, and the GY module's TX drives I/O1 (HARDWARE.md). A hardware SPI test (for example an SDO→SDI loopback with the GY's TX disconnected) needs a bench change approved by Chris.
- **06. Minimal GUI**
  - Features F1, F2 and F4.
- **07. Card framework**
  - Manifest schema and validation, the loader, the card host, and mode activation (F5).
- **08. GY-MCU90640 card, serial driver**
  - Frame parser, checksum, commands and device mock.
  - Hardware test: read one frame in query mode. Needs Chris: this is the first time serial mode drives I/O2 into the module.
- **09. GY-MCU90640 panel**
  - Heatmap and device settings.
- **10. I/O panel (F3)**
- **11. Card editor (F6)**
- **Later:** GY-MCU90640 `i2c_direct`; more cards.

## 7. Out of scope (v1)
- Firmware or bootloader updates.
- Multiple USB-ISS modules at once.
- Editing driver code inside the app.
- Writing to the module's flash in automated tests. Save-to-flash is a manual, confirmed action only.

## 8. Datasheet notes
- **Baud formula (USB-ISS datasheet p.8).** The text prints `48000000/(16+baud)`. The correct formula is `48000000/(16*baud) - 1`, which matches the worked example and the table. Use floor, which matches every table row (19200 gives 155, 9600 gives 311). The actual rate is `48000000/(16*(divisor+1))`.
- **Baud table error (p.8).** The 2400 row lists bytes `0x09 0xE1`, which is 2529. The divisor 1249 is `0x04 0xE1`. Trust the formula, not that row. Add a unit test for it.
- **IO_CHANGE response (resolved).** On hardware, IO_CHANGE in I2C_S_100KHZ returns `FF 00` and leaves the ISS_VERSION mode byte unchanged (iteration 01 hardware logs, firmware 0x09).
- **GETAD on a digital-input pin (erratum, p.20).** The datasheet says a channel that is not set up as analogue returns `0000`. Firmware 0x09 returns the ADC conversion when the pin is a general-I/O digital input. Evidence:
  - **Runner logs.** In 7 of the 8 iteration-02 runner hardware logs, GETAD on I/O1 (digital input) is non-zero. The one `00 00` is consistent with sampling while the module's TX was low (revclaude, iteration 02 fix review).
  - **Unit 1 alone, after a power-cycle, module attached:** `02 E6`, recorded in `claude1-discriminator-hw.txt` as of commit a181b31. That file was later overwritten. The current version contains a failed run, not evidence.
  - **Unit 2** (`claude1-discriminator-hw-unit2.txt`): firmware 0x09, `03 FF`. The log has no runner header. That the unit was serial 00069220 with nothing attached is Chris's statement, not something the log shows.
  - **Unit 1, nothing attached:** `03 D4`, as reported by Chris. The log was lost to the overwrite.
  - Out-of-range channels (0, 5) do return `0000`, as documented. GETAD on output pins and on I2C/serial pins is untested. Other firmware versions are unknown.
- **SETPINS with no output pins (p.20, unspecified).** In IO_MODE with all pins digital input, `63 0F` returns `00` (NACK) (iteration 02 hardware logs).
=====
# Decisions

Format: ID · date · status (adopted / pending Chris / pending claude1) · decision · rationale.

## D-001 · 2026-10-11 · adopted
Language and GUI stack: Python 3.12, PySide6, pyserial, pytest.
Rationale:
- Cross-platform.
- pyserial is the natural fit for the USB-ISS virtual COM port.
- pytest output can be captured directly into the iteration logs.

## D-002 · 2026-10-11 · adopted
Workflow: vsclaude builds, revclaude reviews and writes the next task, claude1 audits at checkpoints. See CLAUDE.md.

## D-003 · 2026-10-11 · adopted
Environment:
- pyenv pins Python 3.12 via a committed `.python-version` file.
- A project venv at `.venv/` (gitignored).
- Dependencies are listed in `pyproject.toml`.
- Never install into, or rely on, the system Python.

Rationale: both Claude Code instances and Chris must run identical interpreters and package versions. A shared system install hides drift.

## D-004 · 2026-10-11 · adopted
Card manifests are JSON (`card.json`). This avoids a YAML dependency, and the GUI card editor (F6) can write it using only the standard library.

## D-005 · 2026-10-16 · adopted

- Valid divisors are 1–255. The calculator never emits 0, because the datasheet says 0 behaves like 1. Requests above 3 MHz or below 23 437.5 Hz are refused.
- The error from the requested SCK is reported, but no error limit is applied. F2's 3% limit applies to serial baud only.

# SPEC — USB-ISS App (v0.1)

claude1 owns the intent of this document. Changes come through checkpoint memos or Chris.

## 1. Purpose
A desktop GUI that:
- gets and sets USB-ISS options;
- operates downstream devices over serial, I2C or SPI through **device cards**.

Cards are the main feature. Everything else exists to support them.

## 2. Stack
Python 3.12, PySide6, pyserial, pytest. See D-001 and D-003.

## 3. Architecture
Four layers. Each layer depends only on the layers below it.

1. **transport**
   - Opens the virtual COM port and does raw byte I/O with timeouts.
   - Has two implementations behind one interface: real (pyserial) and mock.
2. **protocol** (`iss`)
   - Covers every USB-ISS command in the datasheet: ISS setup, I2C, SPI, serial and I/O.
   - Each command is a pure function that builds request bytes, plus a parser for the response.
   - No GUI imports.
3. **cards**
   - Loads card manifests and card drivers.
   - Card drivers talk to their device only through `iss`, never through the transport directly.
4. **gui**
   - Holds the ISS panel (version, serial number, mode, I/O) and a card host, which loads a card's UI panel.

**The mock.**
- The mock USB-ISS emulates the datasheet behaviour: responses, NACK reasons and buffer limits. Where the real device has been shown to contradict the datasheet, the mock follows the device, and §8 records the erratum with its evidence.
- A card may ship a mock of its device, so it can be tested without hardware.

## 4. Features (v1)

**F1. Connect.**
- Pick a port, or take it from `USB_ISS_PORT`.
- Show the module ID, firmware version, current mode and serial number.

**F2. Mode.**
- Set any ISS_MODE from the datasheet, including the combined modes (I2C+Serial, IO+Serial).
- Baud rate is entered in bps. The app computes the divisor and shows the actual rate and the error.
- The app refuses any rate whose error is greater than 3%.

**F3. I/O.**
- Set IO_TYPE per pin, then SETPINS, GETPINS and GETAD.

**F4. Raw console.**
- Send hex bytes and see the response.
- Every frame, in both directions, is shown and logged.

**F5. Cards.**
- Load a card.
- Choose one of its modes.
- The app applies that mode's ISS configuration, then opens the card's panel.

**F6. Card editor.**
- Create or edit a card manifest from the GUI. This covers the metadata, modes, ISS config and resources.
- Driver code is written outside the app; the editor only links to it.

## 5. Device cards

A card is a self-contained directory in `cards/<card-id>/`:

```
cards/gy-mcu90640/
  card.json        manifest (schema below)
  driver.py        one driver class per mode
  panel.py         PySide6 widget(s) for the card UI
  mock.py          optional device mock for tests
  reference/       datasheets and user manuals
  tests/
```

### Manifest (`card.json`)

**Required fields:**
- `id`, `name`, `version`, `description`
- `power`: supply voltage and current draw. The app warns if these exceed what the USB-ISS can supply: 80 mA at 5 V, 30 mA at 3.3 V.
- `resources`: paths into `reference/`
- `modes`: one or more mode entries (below)
- `default_mode`: the id of one entry in `modes`

**Each mode entry has:**
- `id` and `label`
- `status`: `supported` or `planned`. Planned modes are visible in the GUI but can't be activated.
- `iss`: the ISS configuration to apply, given as a mode name plus parameters (baud, io_type, i2c speed, spi phase/divisor).
- `wiring`: a pin map from USB-ISS pins to device pins, shown to the user.
- `driver`: the class name in `driver.py`.
- `device_settings`: device-side options the panel exposes, such as baud, rate or emissivity.

**Principle.** A card should describe *every* way of operating its device, even modes nobody has implemented yet. Once a card has a manifest, a new mode can be added without changing the app.

### First card: GY-MCU90640 (MLX90640 thermal array)

**Mode `serial` (default, supported).**
- ISS configuration: IO_MODE+SERIAL at 115200 baud (divisor 25, actual 115385, error +0.16%).
- Wiring: ISS I/O1 (RX) ← module TX, ISS I/O2 (TX) → module RX, PS left open.
- Device protocol (from the module's user manual):
  - Frames are 1544 bytes: header `5A 5A`, count `0x0602`, then 768 pixel values in little-endian ×100 °C, then Ta, then checksum.
  - The checksum is the 16-bit sum of the first 771 little-endian words.
  - Commands are `A5 <cmd> <arg> <sum8>`, covering baud, rate, query/auto, emissivity, emissivity query and save.
- The driver uses **query mode** by default.
  - Reason: the USB-ISS receive buffer is 62 bytes, so a frame takes at least 25 SERIAL_IO polls.
  - Continuous output is allowed only at 2 Hz or slower.
- 460800 baud is not offered: the divisor would be 5.5 and the error too large.
- Panel:
  - a 32×24 heatmap with the correct pixel order (Col 1/Row 1 is at the upper right);
  - min, max and Ta readouts;
  - device settings;
  - a save-to-flash button behind a confirmation.

**Mode `i2c_direct` (planned).**
- ISS configuration: I2C mode. The module's PS pin is grounded and the module is power-cycled.
- The driver reads the MLX90640 directly, at I2C address 0x33.
- Blocked on two things:
  - the Melexis MLX90640 datasheet (EEPROM calibration and RAM map), which is not yet in `reference/`;
  - confirming the module's I2C logic levels. The module's logic is 3.3 V whatever VIN is: TX measured at 3.3 V with VIN = 5 V.

**Power.**
- The module draws 42 mA, more than the USB-ISS 3.3 V supply can give (30 mA). Its logic is 3.3 V regardless of VIN.
- Supported setup: USB-ISS at 3.3 V (power link removed) so logic levels match; module VIN from a separate 3–5 V supply; grounds shared; USB-ISS VCC pin unconnected (datasheet p.3).
- Do not run the USB-ISS at 5 V with this module. Its 5 V TX would drive the module's 3.3 V RX, and the module's 3.3 V TX may not reliably read as high at the USB-ISS's 5 V input.

## 6. Roadmap
Each item is roughly one iteration. revclaude may split an item, but must not merge two.

- **00. Bootstrap**
  - Package layout and venv setup instructions.
  - A pytest runner that writes `docs/iterations/NN/logs/`.
  - The transport interface with the mock.
  - `iss` ISS_VERSION and GET_SER_NUM, tested against the mock and, read-only, against hardware.
- **01. ISS_MODE**
  - All modes, the IO_TYPE builder, the baud and SPI divisor calculators with error reporting, and NACK parsing.
- **02. SERIAL_IO and I/O commands**
  - SERIAL_IO, SETPINS, GETPINS and GETAD, with buffer limits enforced (30-byte TX, 62-byte RX).
- **03. I2C commands**: I2C_SGL, I2C_AD0/1/2 and I2C_TEST, with frame limits enforced (D-006). Split by revclaude, iteration 02.
- **04. I2C_DIRECT**, with frame limits enforced (D-007). Split by revclaude, iteration 03.
- **05. SPI**, with frame limits enforced. **Mock-only on the current bench:** SPI mode makes I/O1 the CE output, and the GY module's TX drives I/O1 (HARDWARE.md). A hardware SPI test (for example an SDO→SDI loopback with the GY's TX disconnected) needs a bench change approved by Chris.
- **06. Minimal GUI**
  - Features F1, F2 and F4.
- **07. Card framework**
  - Manifest schema and validation, the loader, the card host, and mode activation (F5).
- **08. GY-MCU90640 card, serial driver**
  - Frame parser, checksum, commands and device mock.
  - Hardware test: read one frame in query mode. Needs Chris: this is the first time serial mode drives I/O2 into the module.
- **09. GY-MCU90640 panel**
  - Heatmap and device settings.
- **10. I/O panel (F3)**
- **11. Card editor (F6)**
- **Later:** GY-MCU90640 `i2c_direct`; more cards.

## 7. Out of scope (v1)
- Firmware or bootloader updates.
- Multiple USB-ISS modules at once.
- Editing driver code inside the app.
- Writing to the module's flash in automated tests. Save-to-flash is a manual, confirmed action only.

## 8. Datasheet notes
- **Baud formula (USB-ISS datasheet p.8).** The text prints `48000000/(16+baud)`. The correct formula is `48000000/(16*baud) - 1`, which matches the worked example and the table. Use floor, which matches every table row (19200 gives 155, 9600 gives 311). The actual rate is `48000000/(16*(divisor+1))`.
- **Baud table error (p.8).** The 2400 row lists bytes `0x09 0xE1`, which is 2529. The divisor 1249 is `0x04 0xE1`. Trust the formula, not that row. Add a unit test for it.
- **IO_CHANGE response (resolved).** On hardware, IO_CHANGE in I2C_S_100KHZ returns `FF 00` and leaves the ISS_VERSION mode byte unchanged (iteration 01 hardware logs, firmware 0x09).
- **GETAD on a digital-input pin (erratum, p.20).** The datasheet says a channel that is not set up as analogue returns `0000`. Firmware 0x09 returns the ADC conversion when the pin is a general-I/O digital input. Evidence:
  - **Runner logs.** In 7 of the 8 iteration-02 runner hardware logs, GETAD on I/O1 (digital input) is non-zero. The one `00 00` is consistent with sampling while the module's TX was low (revclaude, iteration 02 fix review).
  - **Unit 1 alone, after a power-cycle, module attached:** `02 E6`, recorded in `claude1-discriminator-hw.txt` as of commit a181b31. That file was later overwritten. The current version contains a failed run, not evidence.
  - **Unit 2** (`claude1-discriminator-hw-unit2.txt`): firmware 0x09, `03 FF`. The log has no runner header. That the unit was serial 00069220 with nothing attached is Chris's statement, not something the log shows.
  - **Unit 1, nothing attached:** `03 D4`, as reported by Chris. The log was lost to the overwrite.
  - Out-of-range channels (0, 5) do return `0000`, as documented. GETAD on output pins and on I2C/serial pins is untested. Other firmware versions are unknown.
- **SETPINS with no output pins (p.20, unspecified).** In IO_MODE with all pins digital input, `63 0F` returns `00` (NACK) (iteration 02 hardware logs).

# Bench hardware

Chris owns this file. It describes what is physically connected to the USB-ISS right now. Read it before any hardware test. A `NEXT.md` hardware section must be consistent with it. If they disagree, stop and report the conflict.

Last updated: 2026-10-17 (claude1, from Chris's measurements). **Bench changed after iteration 02:** the USB-ISS now runs at 3.3 V. Hardware logs from iterations 00–02 were taken at 5 V.

## USB-ISS
- Connected to the PC over USB, which also powers it. The port comes from `USB_ISS_PORT` in `.env`.
- **The 5 V power link is removed, so the USB-ISS runs at 3.3 V.** VCC measured 3.3 V. Logic levels are 3.3 V. Inputs are **not** 5 V tolerant (datasheet p.3).
- The bootloader link is not fitted. Never fit it.
- The VCC pin is **not connected** to anything. Never apply an external voltage to it (p.3).
- GETAD full scale (1023) now corresponds to 3.3 V.
- The bench unit is firmware 0x09, serial 00069221, and `.env` points to it.
- A second USB-ISS, serial 00069220 (firmware 0x09), is available but not normally connected. It was used once in iteration 02 to cross-check the GETAD erratum.
- **The `.env` setting is copied into each VS Code terminal when the terminal opens** (`python.terminal.useEnvFile`), and the environment variable takes priority over `.env`. After you edit `.env`, open a new terminal. To use a different port for one run, set it on the command line: `USB_ISS_PORT=... <command>`.

## Attached: GY-MCU90640, serial mode (card `gy-mcu90640`, mode `serial`)

| GY pin | Connects to | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| VIN | separate 5 V supply (measured 5.0 V) | 100 nF (104) capacitor across VIN and GND. 42 mA draw. |
| GND | supply GND **and** USB-ISS GND | Common ground. |
| TX | USB-ISS I/O1 | USB-ISS RX in serial modes. **Driven by the module**, 3.3 V high (measured). |
| RX | USB-ISS I/O2 | USB-ISS TX in serial modes. 3.3 V logic on both sides. |
| SCL, SDA | not connected | These pins are the MLX90640's own I2C bus. With PS open, the module's MCU is the master on that bus. Never connect them to the USB-ISS in this mode. |
| PS | open | Serial mode. Grounding PS and power-cycling selects I2C-direct mode (GY manual p.5). |

### Consequences for tests
- I/O1 is driven by the module's TX. At power-up the module transmits continuously at 115200 baud, as confirmed on a scope (2026-10-17). **Never configure I/O1 as an output.** In IO_MODE, GETPINS and GETAD on I/O1 return varying values, including `00 00` when sampled while TX is low. Log them, don't assert them.
- While I/O2 is an input, the RX line is undriven. It sits near 2.4 V and picks up crosstalk from TX (scope, 2026-10-17). This is harmless, and in serial modes the USB-ISS drives it.
- In serial modes the USB-ISS drives I/O2 (TX) into the module's RX. Any byte sent is a command to the module (GY manual §IV). Send only commands that `NEXT.md` names explicitly. Never send save-to-flash in automated tests (SPEC §7).
- I/O3 and I/O4 (SCL and SDA in I2C modes) are unconnected. The I2C bus is empty, and the USB-ISS's 4.7k pull-ups hold it at 3.3 V.
- In every IO_TYPE byte, set unused pin pairs to digital input (`10`), never output (`00`/`01`).

## Not attached
- A second GY-MCU90640 with PS grounded (I2C direct). It was removed on 2026-10-17 because two modules would exceed the 80 mA power budget. Iteration 01's hardware runs were taken with both modules attached and the I2C lines shared.

# Bench hardware

Chris owns this file. It describes what is physically connected to the USB-ISS right now. Read it before any hardware test. A `NEXT.md` hardware section must be consistent with it. If they disagree, stop and report the conflict.

Last updated: 2026-10-17 (claude1, from Chris's measurements). **Bench changed after iteration 02:** the USB-ISS now runs at 3.3 V. Hardware logs from iterations 00–02 were taken at 5 V.

## USB-ISS
- Connected to the PC over USB, which also powers it. The port comes from `USB_ISS_PORT` in `.env`.
- **The 5 V power link is removed, so the USB-ISS runs at 3.3 V.** VCC measured 3.3 V. Logic levels are 3.3 V. Inputs are **not** 5 V tolerant (datasheet p.3).
- The bootloader link is not fitted. Never fit it.
- The VCC pin is **not connected** to anything. Never apply an external voltage to it (p.3).
- GETAD full scale (1023) now corresponds to 3.3 V.
- The bench unit is firmware 0x09, serial 00069221, and `.env` points to it.
- A second USB-ISS, serial 00069220 (firmware 0x09), is available but not normally connected. It was used once in iteration 02 to cross-check the GETAD erratum.
- **The `.env` setting is copied into each VS Code terminal when the terminal opens** (`python.terminal.useEnvFile`), and the environment variable takes priority over `.env`. After you edit `.env`, open a new terminal. To use a different port for one run, set it on the command line: `USB_ISS_PORT=... <command>`.

## Attached: GY-MCU90640, serial mode (card `gy-mcu90640`, mode `serial`)

| GY pin | Connects to | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| VIN | separate 5 V supply (measured 5.0 V) | 100 nF (104) capacitor across VIN and GND. 42 mA draw. |
| GND | supply GND **and** USB-ISS GND | Common ground. |
| TX | USB-ISS I/O1 | USB-ISS RX in serial modes. **Driven by the module**, 3.3 V high (measured). |
| RX | USB-ISS I/O2 | USB-ISS TX in serial modes. 3.3 V logic on both sides. |
| SCL, SDA | not connected | These pins are the MLX90640's own I2C bus. With PS open, the module's MCU is the master on that bus. Never connect them to the USB-ISS in this mode. |
| PS | open | Serial mode. Grounding PS and power-cycling selects I2C-direct mode (GY manual p.5). |

### Consequences for tests
- I/O1 is driven by the module's TX. At power-up the module transmits continuously at 115200 baud, as confirmed on a scope (2026-10-17). **Never configure I/O1 as an output.** In IO_MODE, GETPINS and GETAD on I/O1 return varying values, including `00 00` when sampled while TX is low. Log them, don't assert them.
- While I/O2 is an input, the RX line is undriven. It sits near 2.4 V and picks up crosstalk from TX (scope, 2026-10-17). This is harmless, and in serial modes the USB-ISS drives it.
- In serial modes the USB-ISS drives I/O2 (TX) into the module's RX. Any byte sent is a command to the module (GY manual §IV). Send only commands that `NEXT.md` names explicitly. Never send save-to-flash in automated tests (SPEC §7).
- I/O3 and I/O4 (SCL and SDA in I2C modes) are unconnected. The I2C bus is empty, and the USB-ISS's 4.7k pull-ups hold it at 3.3 V.
- In every IO_TYPE byte, set unused pin pairs to digital input (`10`), never output (`00`/`01`).

## Not attached
- A second GY-MCU90640 with PS grounded (I2C direct). It was removed on 2026-10-17 because two modules would exceed the 80 mA power budget. Iteration 01's hardware runs were taken with both modules attached and the I2C lines shared.

### 1.3 Reviewer misses
These are defects revclaude passed that surfaced later: #3 (its own NEXT), #5 (passed twice), #8.

On GETAD, revclaude reached the right erratum without ruling out the state hypothesis. claude1's competing hypothesis was then **refuted** by the power-cycle discriminator, so claude1 was wrong on that point.

Pattern: **revclaude is strong at reading code and records** (#10 and #12, 11/11 mutants killed in iteration 03). **It is weaker on hardware consequences in its own NEXTs** (#3, #7).

### 1.4 claude1's own defects
#4 (unverified handoff) and #10 (overwritten log, then cited). The fixes are now standard practice:
- claude1 confirms each edit on `origin` before saying go;
- no `tee` to a fixed file name.

### 1.5 Increment sizing
Good. revclaude split roadmap item 03 and item 04, each correctly, and the builder averages about one iteration per session.

These match the datasheet:
- ISS_VERSION and GET_SER_NUM (p.5);
- ISS_MODE frames and responses (pp.6–10);
- the baud formula and table, where only the 2400 row is wrong (p.8);
- the SPI divisor (p.10);

- GETAD converts on a digital-input pin (2 units, fw 0x09);
- SETPINS with no outputs returns NACK;
- IO_CHANGE returns `FF 00`;
- an empty-bus I2C read returns `FF`;
- I2C_TEST on an absent device returns `00`, also in IO_MODE.

- No byte has been received from the GY module over the USB-ISS. The scope shows its TX running at 115200.

  - 04 I2C_DIRECT;

  - 06 GUI;
  - 07 card framework;
  - 08 GY serial driver, which needs Chris because it is the first time anything is sent to the module;
  - 09 GY panel;
  - 10 I/O panel;
  - 11 card editor.
- **D-007 ratified.**
- **SPI on hardware stays mock-only** until Chris approves a bench change (for example an SDO→SDI loopback with GY TX disconnected). This is Chris's call. The default is mock-only.

### 3.1 The experiment
Only one process variable changes: who drives the steps between checkpoints. The script does instead of Chris. Models and efforts stay the same (Sonnet builder, Opus/high reviewer, and the effort recommended in NEXT).

- **Confirmed at CP-02 if both hold:**

- **Refuted if either holds:**

- **D-007: adopted.**

- Fill in Chris minutes for LOG rows 02/1 and 03.
- Run the loop from a plain terminal in the repo root: `./scripts/loop.sh`. For phone alerts, set `NTFY_TOPIC` first.
- Leave the bench alone while the loop runs.

# Role: vsclaude (builder)

Recommended model and effort: Sonnet 5.5, medium. If `NEXT.md` asks for something else (for example Opus 5.5, high) and you are not running on it, tell Chris before you start.

## Each iteration (`/build`)
1. Read `NEXT.md`, the SPEC sections and datasheet sections it cites, and, if this is a fix cycle, the latest `review.md` in `docs/iterations/NN/`.
2. If anything is ambiguous or contradictory, stop. Write your questions in the build report rather than guessing.
3. Check out branch `iter/NN`, creating it if needed.
4. Implement only what `NEXT.md` scopes.

7. Commit, then stop and tell Chris: "Iteration NN built — ready for /review."

## Rules
- Do not edit SPEC, DECISIONS, NEXT, the role files, the templates, LOG or CHANGES. Put any proposed changes in your report.
- Never weaken, skip or delete a test to get a green run. If you think a test is wrong, say so in the report.
- Report every deviation from `NEXT.md`. A deviation you report is fine; one you hide is a defect.
- In protocol code, each command should cite the datasheet section it implements, in a comment. Use printed page numbers (the `N/23` footer).
- Run Python only as `.venv/bin/python` (the runner or `-m pytest`).
- Don't install, upgrade or configure anything outside the repo: no pip, pyenv or system packages. If you need to, stop and report it as a blocker.
- Never delete, move or overwrite a log. Superseded or failed runs stay, and `build.md` explains each one.
- In a headless run (`scripts/loop.sh`), commands outside the allow list are denied. Treat a denial as a blocker. Don't work around it.
- If you stop with questions or a blocker, report `status: blocked` when the loop asks for a structured result.

+# ---- I2C_DIRECT, datasheet pp.15-16; D-007 ----
+I2C_DIRECT = 0x57  # p.15
+I2C_DIRECT_START = 0x01  # p.15
+I2C_DIRECT_RESTART = 0x02  # p.15
+I2C_DIRECT_STOP = 0x03  # p.15
+I2C_DIRECT_NACK = 0x04  # p.15: send NACK after the next read
+I2C_DIRECT_READ_BASE = 0x20  # p.15: READ 0x20-0x2F reads 1-16 bytes
+I2C_DIRECT_WRITE_BASE = 0x30  # p.15: WRITE 0x30-0x3F writes the next 1-16 bytes
+I2C_DIRECT_FRAME_MAX = 59  # D-007: the whole frame, 0x57 included (p.15: "< 60 bytes")
+I2C_DIRECT_CHUNK_MAX = 16  # p.15: bytes per READ or WRITE sub-command
+I2C_DIRECT_READ_TOTAL_MAX = 60  # D-007: the datasheet gives no limit; closest documented read limit (p.13)
+I2C_DIRECT_NACK_REASONS = {0x01: "Device Error", 0x02: "Buffer Overflow", 0x03: "Buffer Underflow", 0x04: "Unknown command"}  # p.15
+
+
+# READ, p.15: one sub-command byte, 0x20 + n - 1.
+def direct_read(n: int) -> bytes:
+    if not 1 <= n <= I2C_DIRECT_CHUNK_MAX:
+        raise ValueError(f"I2C_DIRECT READ: byte count {n} outside 1-{I2C_DIRECT_CHUNK_MAX}")
+    return bytes([I2C_DIRECT_READ_BASE + n - 1])
+
+
+# WRITE, p.15: sub-command byte 0x30 + n - 1, then the n bytes. The device address is written like any other byte.
+def direct_write(data: bytes) -> bytes:
+    if not 1 <= len(data) <= I2C_DIRECT_CHUNK_MAX:
+        raise ValueError(f"I2C_DIRECT WRITE: byte count {len(data)} outside 1-{I2C_DIRECT_CHUNK_MAX}")
+    return bytes([I2C_DIRECT_WRITE_BASE + len(data) - 1]) + bytes(data)
+
+
+def _direct_walk(frame: bytes) -> tuple[int, int]:
+    """Walk the sub-commands after the 0x57 byte. Returns (sub-command count, total READ bytes)."""
+    subs = reads = 0
+    i = 1
+    while i < len(frame):
+        sub = frame[i]
+        subs += 1
+        i += 1
+        if I2C_DIRECT_START <= sub <= I2C_DIRECT_NACK:
+            continue
+        if 0x20 <= sub <= 0x2F:
+            reads += sub - I2C_DIRECT_READ_BASE + 1
+        elif 0x30 <= sub <= 0x3F:
+            k = sub - I2C_DIRECT_WRITE_BASE + 1
+            if len(frame) - i < k:
+                raise ValueError(f"I2C_DIRECT: WRITE 0x{sub:02X} needs {k} data bytes, only {len(frame) - i} follow")
+            i += k
+        else:
+            raise ValueError(f"I2C_DIRECT: 0x{sub:02X} is not a sub-command")
+    return subs, reads
+
+
+# I2C_DIRECT, p.15: 57 followed by sub-commands. Checks the frame structure and D-007's limits, not I2C semantics.
+def build_i2c_direct(*parts: int | bytes) -> bytes:
+    frame = bytearray([I2C_DIRECT])
+    for part in parts:
+        if isinstance(part, int):
+            frame.append(_byte(part, "I2C_DIRECT sub-command"))
+        else:
+            frame += part
+    frame = bytes(frame)
+    subs, reads = _direct_walk(frame)
+    if subs == 0:
+        raise ValueError("I2C_DIRECT: no sub-commands")
+    if len(frame) > I2C_DIRECT_FRAME_MAX:
+        raise ValueError(f"I2C_DIRECT: frame of {len(frame)} bytes exceeds {I2C_DIRECT_FRAME_MAX}")
+    if reads > I2C_DIRECT_READ_TOTAL_MAX:
+        raise ValueError(f"I2C_DIRECT: {reads} bytes read exceeds {I2C_DIRECT_READ_TOTAL_MAX}")
+    return frame
+
+
+def i2c_direct_read_count(frame: bytes) -> int:
+    """Total bytes the READ sub-commands of a built frame will return."""
+    return _direct_walk(frame)[1]
+
+
+def parse_i2c_direct_status(resp: bytes) -> int:
+    """I2C_DIRECT status bytes, p.15: FF nn is ACK with nn bytes to read; 00 rr is NACK with reason rr."""
+    if len(resp) < 2:
+        raise IssTimeout(f"I2C_DIRECT: expected 2 status bytes, got {len(resp)}")
+    if resp[0] == 0xFF:
+        return resp[1]
+    if resp[0] == 0x00:
+        raise IssNack(resp[1], "I2C_DIRECT")
+    raise IssProtocolError(f"I2C_DIRECT: first byte 0x{resp[0]:02X} is neither ACK nor NACK")
+
+
+def i2c_direct(transport: Transport, *parts: int | bytes) -> bytes:
+    frame = build_i2c_direct(*parts)
+    transport.write(frame)  # one write(): the device ends a frame at an inter-byte gap (D-007)
+    n = parse_i2c_direct_status(transport.read(2))
+    data = transport.read(n) if n else b""
+    if len(data) < n:
+        raise IssTimeout(f"I2C_DIRECT: expected {n} data bytes, got {len(data)}")
+    expected = i2c_direct_read_count(frame)
+    if n != expected:
+        raise IssProtocolError(f"I2C_DIRECT: device reports {n} bytes, frame reads {expected}")
+    return bytes(data)

@@ -0,0 +1,274 @@
+"""Iteration 04: I2C_DIRECT (datasheet pp.15-16; D-007)."""
+import pytest
+
+from usb_iss_app import iss
+from usb_iss_app.mock import MockI2cDevice, MockTransport
+
+B = bytes.fromhex
+STOP = iss.I2C_DIRECT_STOP
+
+
+def test_constants():
+    assert iss.I2C_DIRECT == 0x57
+    assert (iss.I2C_DIRECT_START, iss.I2C_DIRECT_RESTART, iss.I2C_DIRECT_STOP, iss.I2C_DIRECT_NACK) == (1, 2, 3, 4)
+    assert (iss.I2C_DIRECT_FRAME_MAX, iss.I2C_DIRECT_CHUNK_MAX, iss.I2C_DIRECT_READ_TOTAL_MAX) == (59, 16, 60)
+    assert iss.I2C_DIRECT_NACK_REASONS == {1: "Device Error", 2: "Buffer Overflow", 3: "Buffer Underflow", 4: "Unknown command"}
+
+
+# ---- builders: datasheet examples ----
+def test_example_pcf8574_write():  # p.15
+    assert iss.build_i2c_direct(1, iss.direct_write(B("40 55")), 3) == B("57 01 31 40 55 03")
+
+
+def test_example_24lc512_write():  # p.16, nn nn = 12 34
+    frame = iss.build_i2c_direct(1, iss.direct_write(B("A0 00 00 12 34")), 3)
+    assert frame == B("57 01 34 A0 00 00 12 34 03")
+
+
+def test_example_read_with_nack():  # p.16
+    frame = iss.build_i2c_direct(1, iss.direct_write(B("A0 00 00")), 2, iss.direct_write(b"\xA1"),
+                                 iss.direct_read(3), 4, iss.direct_read(1), 3)
+    assert frame == B("57 01 32 A0 00 00 02 30 A1 22 04 20 03")
+    assert iss.i2c_direct_read_count(frame) == 4
+
+
+def test_example_read():  # p.16
+    frame = iss.build_i2c_direct(1, iss.direct_write(B("A0 00 00")), 2, iss.direct_write(b"\xA1"),
+                                 iss.direct_read(4), 3)
+    assert frame == B("57 01 32 A0 00 00 02 30 A1 23 03")
+    assert iss.i2c_direct_read_count(frame) == 4
+
+
+# ---- limits ----
+def test_direct_read_limits():
+    assert iss.direct_read(1) == B("20") and iss.direct_read(16) == B("2F")
+    for n in (0, 17):
+        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
+            iss.direct_read(n)
+
+
+def test_direct_write_limits():
+    assert iss.direct_write(b"\1") == B("30 01")
+    assert iss.direct_write(bytes(16)) == B("3F") + bytes(16)
+    for data in (b"", bytes(17)):
+        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
+            iss.direct_write(data)
+
+
+def test_frame_length_boundary():
+    assert len(iss.build_i2c_direct(*[STOP] * 58)) == 59
+    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
+        iss.build_i2c_direct(*[STOP] * 59)
+
+
+def test_total_read_boundary():
+    r = iss.direct_read
+    frame = iss.build_i2c_direct(r(16), r(16), r(16), r(12))
+    assert iss.i2c_direct_read_count(frame) == 60
+    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
+        iss.build_i2c_direct(r(16), r(16), r(16), r(13))
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("parts", [(), (0x00,), (0x05,), (0x1F,), (0x40,), (256,), (-1,),
+                                   (0x31, b"\x40"), (0x30,)])
+def test_refused_frames(parts):
+    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
+        iss.build_i2c_direct(*parts)
+
+
+# ---- NACK names and parser ----
+def test_parse_status_ack():
+    assert iss.parse_i2c_direct_status(B("FF 00")) == 0
+    assert iss.parse_i2c_direct_status(B("FF 04")) == 4
+
+
+@pytest.mark.parametrize("rr,name", [(1, "Device Error"), (2, "Buffer Overflow"), (3, "Buffer Underflow"),
+                                     (4, "Unknown command")])
+def test_parse_status_nack(rr, name):
+    with pytest.raises(iss.IssNack, match=f"I2C_DIRECT NACK: 0x{rr:02X} {name}") as e:
+        iss.parse_i2c_direct_status(bytes([0, rr]))
+    assert e.value.reason == rr and e.value.name == name
+
+
+def test_parse_status_errors():
+    for resp in (B("00"), b""):
+        with pytest.raises(iss.IssTimeout):
+            iss.parse_i2c_direct_status(resp)
+    with pytest.raises(iss.IssProtocolError):
+        iss.parse_i2c_direct_status(B("7F 00"))
+
+
+def test_iss_mode_nack_names_unchanged():
+    with pytest.raises(iss.IssNack, match="ISS_MODE NACK: 0x05 Unknown command"):
+        iss.parse_mode_response(B("00 05"))
+    assert "Internal Error 1" in str(iss.IssNack(6))
+
+
+# ---- helper ----
+class _Short(MockTransport):
+    """Answers every I2C_DIRECT with a canned reply."""
+    def __init__(self, reply):
+        super().__init__(mode=0x40)
+        self.reply = reply
+        self.writes = []
+
+    def write(self, data):
+        self.writes.append(bytes(data))
+        self._rx += self.reply
+
+
+def test_helper_single_write():
+    t = _Short(B("FF 00"))
+    iss.i2c_direct(t, 1, iss.direct_write(B("40 55")), 3)
+    assert t.writes == [B("57 01 31 40 55 03")]
+
+
+def test_helper_short_data_times_out():
+    with pytest.raises(iss.IssTimeout):
+        iss.i2c_direct(_Short(B("FF 02 AA")), iss.direct_read(2))
+
+
+def test_helper_count_mismatch_reads_everything():
+    t = _Short(B("FF 03 01 02 03"))
+    with pytest.raises(iss.IssProtocolError):
+        iss.i2c_direct(t, iss.direct_read(2))
+    assert t.read(1) == b""  # nothing left behind
+
+
+# ---- mock ----
+def bus(devices=None, mode=0x40):
+    m = MockTransport(mode=mode)
+    m.i2c_devices = dict(devices or {})
+    return m
+
+
+def write_frame(*data):
+    return iss.build_i2c_direct(1, iss.direct_write(bytes(data)), 3)
+
+
+def test_mock_pcf8574_write():
+    d = MockI2cDevice(addr_bytes=0)
+    m = bus({0x40: d})
+    assert iss.i2c_direct(m, 1, iss.direct_write(B("40 55")), 3) == b""
+    assert d.mem[0] == 0x55
+
+
+def eeprom():
+    d = MockI2cDevice(size=0x10000, addr_bytes=2)
+    d.mem[2:4] = B("56 78")
+    return d
+
+
+def test_mock_24lc512_write_and_reads():
+    d = eeprom()
+    m = bus({0xA0: d})
+    assert iss.i2c_direct(m, 1, iss.direct_write(B("A0 00 00 12 34")), 3) == b""
+    assert d.mem[0:4] == B("12 34 56 78")
+    sel = (1, iss.direct_write(B("A0 00 00")), 2, iss.direct_write(b"\xA1"))
+    assert iss.i2c_direct(m, *sel, iss.direct_read(3), 4, iss.direct_read(1), 3) == B("12 34 56 78")
+    assert iss.i2c_direct(m, *sel, iss.direct_read(4), 3) == B("12 34 56 78")
+
+
+def test_mock_direct_write_read_back_by_ad1():
+    m = bus({0xA0: MockI2cDevice(addr_bytes=1)})
+    iss.i2c_direct(m, 1, iss.direct_write(B("A0 07 11 22")), 3)
+    assert iss.i2c_ad1_read(m, 0xA0, 7, 2) == B("11 22")
+
+
+def test_mock_partial_pointer_does_not_set_pointer():
+    d = MockI2cDevice(size=0x10000, addr_bytes=2)
+    d.pointer = 5
+    m = bus({0xA0: d})
+    iss.i2c_direct(m, 1, iss.direct_write(B("A0 12")), 3)
+    assert d.pointer == 5
+
+
+def test_mock_absent_address_nacks_reason_1():
+    m = bus()
+    with pytest.raises(iss.IssNack) as e:
+        iss.i2c_direct(m, 1, iss.direct_write(b"\xA0"), 3)
+    assert e.value.reason == 1
+
+
+def test_mock_read_without_device_is_ff():
+    m = bus()
+    assert iss.i2c_direct(m, iss.direct_read(3)) == B("FF FF FF")
+
+
+def test_mock_underflow():
+    m = bus({0x40: MockI2cDevice()})
+    m.write(B("57 01 31 40"))
+    assert m.read(4) == B("00 03")
+
+
+def test_mock_unknown_subcommand_is_ignored():
+    # Hardware (build-hw-20261018-021131): 57 05 answers FF 00, not 00 04.
+    m = bus()
+    m.write(B("57 05"))
+    assert m.read(4) == B("FF 00")
+
+
+def test_mock_frame_length_boundary():
+    m = bus()
+    # Hardware (build-hw-20261018-021131): 60 bytes still answers FF 00, so the mock overflows at 61.
+    m.write(B("57") + bytes([STOP]) * 60)
+    assert m.read(4) == B("00 02")
+    m.write(B("57") + bytes([STOP]) * 59)
+    assert m.read(4) == B("FF 00")
+    m.write(B("57") + bytes([STOP]) * 58)
+    assert m.read(4) == B("FF 00")
+
+
+def test_mock_overflow_executes_nothing():
+    d = MockI2cDevice(addr_bytes=0)
+    m = bus({0x40: d})
+    m.write(B("57 01 31 40 55") + bytes([STOP]) * 56)  # 61 bytes
+    assert m.read(4) == B("00 02")
+    assert d.mem[0] == 0
+
+
+def test_mock_split_frame():
+    m = bus({0x40: MockI2cDevice()})
+    m.write(B("57 01 31"))
+    assert m.read(4) == B("00 03")
+    # 40 is dropped; 55 03 then starts an I2C_AD1 frame, which stays pending like on the device.
+    m.write(B("40 55 03"))
+    assert m.read(4) == b""
+    assert m.unhandled == [B("40")]
+
+
+def test_mock_5a_01_is_data():
+    d = MockI2cDevice(addr_bytes=0)
+    m = bus({0x40: d})
+    assert iss.i2c_direct(m, 1, iss.direct_write(B("40 5A 01")), 3) == b""
+    assert d.mem[0:2] == B("5A 01")
+    assert m.unhandled == [] and m.read(3) == b""
+
+
+def test_mock_i2c_serial_mode():
+    d = MockI2cDevice(addr_bytes=1)
+    m = bus({0xA0: d})
+    iss.set_mode(m, iss.build_i2c_serial(iss.I2C_S_100KHZ, 9600))
+    iss.i2c_direct(m, 1, iss.direct_write(B("A0 03 99")), 3)
+    assert d.mem[3] == 0x99
+
+
+def test_mock_io_mode_answers_00():
+    # Hardware (build-hw-20261018-021131): in IO_MODE, 57 01 30 A0 03 answers a single 00.
+    m = bus({0x40: MockI2cDevice()})
+    iss.set_mode(m, iss.build_io_mode(0xAA))
+    m.write(B("57 01 30 40 03"))
+    assert m.read(4) == B("00")
+    with pytest.raises(iss.IssTimeout):
+        iss.i2c_direct(m, 1, iss.direct_write(b"\x40"), 3)  # 00 alone is one status byte
+    assert m.unhandled == []
+    assert iss.version(m).mode == 0x00
+
+
+def test_mock_io_serial_mode_consumes_frame():
+    m = bus({0x40: MockI2cDevice()})
+    iss.set_mode(m, iss.build_io_serial(9600, 0xAA))
+    with pytest.raises(iss.IssTimeout):
+        iss.i2c_direct(m, 1, iss.direct_write(b"\x40"), 3)
+    assert m.unhandled == [B("57 01 30 40 03")]
+    assert iss.version(m).mode == 0x01

/usr/bin/pdftotext
I2C_DIRECT commands
The I2C_DIRECT commands are used to build custom I2C sequences. You send the I2C_DIRECT command (0x57)
followed by as many sub-commands as required.
These sub-commands are:

START             0x01             send start sequence
RESTART           0x02             send restart sequence
STOP              0x03             send stop sequence
NACK              0x04             send NACK after next read
READ              0x20 - 0x2F      reads 1-16 bytes
WRITE             0x30 - 0x3F      writes next 1-16 bytes


The I2C_Read sub-commands can read up to 16 bytes. 0x20 will read 1 byte, 0x21 will read 2 bytes, 0x2F will read 16
bytes. All bytes read are buffered and sent after all sub-commands are processed.
The I2C_Write sub-commands can write up to 16 bytes. 0x30 will write 1 byte, 0x35 will write 6 bytes, 0x3F will write
16 bytes. The bytes to be written immediately follow the write sub-command.
It is up to you to make sure you supply the correct number of bytes as specified in the sub-command.
The response to the I2C_DIRECT command is a variable number of bytes, but it will always be at least two. You should
read these two bytes first as they are the status bytes.
The fist byte is the ACK (0xFF) or NACK (0x00) status.
If you get an ACK the command was successful and the second byte contains the number of bytes to read. If you have
not requested any reads then it will be zero, otherwise you should now read the number of bytes available.
If you get a NACK the command failed and the second byte contains the reason, as follows:

Error Type                 Error Code       Comment
Device Error               0x01             No ACK from device
Buffer Overflow            0x02             You must limit the frame to < 60 bytes
Buffer Underflow           0x03             More write data was expected than sent
Unknown command            0x04             Probably your write count is wrong


Here is the sequence to write 0x55 to the PCF8574 I/O expander:

Direct    Start     Write       Address Data    Stop
0x57      0x01      0x31        0x40    0x55 0x03




© Devantech Ltd 23/3/2026                 USB-ISS Documentation                                         15/23
 The following will write 2 bytes to a 24LC512 EEPROM. This uses 2 internal address bytes.

Direct    Start     Write I2C     Address Address Data 1 Data 2 STOP
                          Address high    low
0x57      0x01      0x34 0xA0        0x00     0x00     0xnn        0xnn     0x03

And this will read 4 bytes from a 24LC512 EEPROM.

 Direct Start      Write I2C     Address Address Restart Write I2C     Read nack Read Stop
                         Address High    Low                   Address
 0x57     0x01     0x32    0xA0      0x00     0x00     0x02        0x30 0xA1        0x22 0x04 0x20 0x03

Note that as part of the read sequence we first have to write the address that we want to read from. We read
3of the 4 bytes then set the NACK flag before reading the last byte. This is according to I2C specifications,
however its not really necessary and the following will work just as well:

 Direct Start      Write   I2C       Address Address     Restart    Write    I2C       Read    Stop
                           Address   High    Low                             Address
 0x57    0x01      0x32    0xA0      0x00     0x00       0x02       0x30     0xA1      0x23    0x03


Checking for the existence of an I2C device
(V5 and later firmware only)

I2C_TEST        Device Address
0x58            0xA0

This 2 byte command was added to V5 following customer requests. It checks for the ACK response to a
devices address. A single byte is returned, zero if no device is detected or non-zero if the device was detected.




© Devantech Ltd 23/3/2026               USB-ISS Documentation                                         16/23

I2C_DIRECT commands
The I2C_DIRECT commands are used to build custom I2C sequences. You send the I2C_DIRECT command (0x57)
followed by as many sub-commands as required.
These sub-commands are:

START             0x01             send start sequence
RESTART           0x02             send restart sequence
STOP              0x03             send stop sequence
NACK              0x04             send NACK after next read
READ              0x20 - 0x2F      reads 1-16 bytes
WRITE             0x30 - 0x3F      writes next 1-16 bytes


The I2C_Read sub-commands can read up to 16 bytes. 0x20 will read 1 byte, 0x21 will read 2 bytes, 0x2F will read 16
bytes. All bytes read are buffered and sent after all sub-commands are processed.
The I2C_Write sub-commands can write up to 16 bytes. 0x30 will write 1 byte, 0x35 will write 6 bytes, 0x3F will write
16 bytes. The bytes to be written immediately follow the write sub-command.
It is up to you to make sure you supply the correct number of bytes as specified in the sub-command.
The response to the I2C_DIRECT command is a variable number of bytes, but it will always be at least two. You should
read these two bytes first as they are the status bytes.
The fist byte is the ACK (0xFF) or NACK (0x00) status.
If you get an ACK the command was successful and the second byte contains the number of bytes to read. If you have
not requested any reads then it will be zero, otherwise you should now read the number of bytes available.
If you get a NACK the command failed and the second byte contains the reason, as follows:

Error Type                 Error Code       Comment
Device Error               0x01             No ACK from device
Buffer Overflow            0x02             You must limit the frame to < 60 bytes
Buffer Underflow           0x03             More write data was expected than sent
Unknown command            0x04             Probably your write count is wrong


Here is the sequence to write 0x55 to the PCF8574 I/O expander:

Direct    Start     Write       Address Data    Stop
0x57      0x01      0x31        0x40    0x55 0x03




© Devantech Ltd 23/3/2026                 USB-ISS Documentation                                         15/23
 The following will write 2 bytes to a 24LC512 EEPROM. This uses 2 internal address bytes.

Direct    Start     Write I2C     Address Address Data 1 Data 2 STOP
                          Address high    low
0x57      0x01      0x34 0xA0        0x00     0x00     0xnn        0xnn     0x03

And this will read 4 bytes from a 24LC512 EEPROM.

 Direct Start      Write I2C     Address Address Restart Write I2C     Read nack Read Stop
                         Address High    Low                   Address
 0x57     0x01     0x32    0xA0      0x00     0x00     0x02        0x30 0xA1        0x22 0x04 0x20 0x03

Note that as part of the read sequence we first have to write the address that we want to read from. We read
3of the 4 bytes then set the NACK flag before reading the last byte. This is according to I2C specifications,
however its not really necessary and the following will work just as well:

 Direct Start      Write   I2C       Address Address     Restart    Write    I2C       Read    Stop
                           Address   High    Low                             Address
 0x57    0x01      0x32    0xA0      0x00     0x00       0x02       0x30     0xA1      0x23    0x03


Checking for the existence of an I2C device
(V5 and later firmware only)

I2C_TEST        Device Address
0x58            0xA0

This 2 byte command was added to V5 following customer requests. It checks for the ACK response to a
devices address. A single byte is returned, zero if no device is detected or non-zero if the device was detected.




© Devantech Ltd 23/3/2026               USB-ISS Documentation                                         16/23

# Hardware: a 60-byte I2C_DIRECT frame (0x57 plus 59 STOPs) answered FF 00, so the device accepts at least
# 60 bytes (docs/iterations/04/logs/build-hw-20261018-021131.txt). The builder limit stays at 59 (D-007).
# ASSUMPTION: longer frames overflow, as p.15 says; 61 bytes has not been tried.
MOCK_DIRECT_OVERFLOW = 60


class MockI2cDevice:
    """A test-defined I2C slave: memory plus a pointer that post-increments and wraps at size.

    addr_bytes (0, 1 or 2) is the number of internal address bytes that I2C_DIRECT writes send
    before data (pp.15-16). Only I2C_DIRECT uses it; the register commands set the pointer themselves.
    """

    def __init__(self, size: int = 256, addr_bytes: int = 1):
        if addr_bytes not in (0, 1, 2):
            raise ValueError(f"addr_bytes {addr_bytes} is not 0, 1 or 2")
        self.size = size
        self.addr_bytes = addr_bytes
        self.mem = bytearray(size)
        self.pointer = 0
        self._addr_buf = bytearray()

    def begin_direct_write(self) -> None:
        """A write transaction starts (I2C_DIRECT): the next addr_bytes bytes set the pointer."""
        self._addr_buf.clear()

    def direct_write(self, data: bytes) -> None:
        """I2C_DIRECT write bytes: pointer bytes first, high byte first, then data at the pointer."""
        for b in data:
            if len(self._addr_buf) < self.addr_bytes:
                self._addr_buf.append(b)
                if len(self._addr_buf) == self.addr_bytes:
                    self.pointer = int.from_bytes(self._addr_buf, "big") % self.size
            else:
                self.write(bytes([b]))

    def write(self, data: bytes) -> None:
        for b in data:
            self.mem[self.pointer] = b
            self.pointer = (self.pointer + 1) % self.size

    def read(self, n: int) -> bytes:
        out = bytearray()
        for _ in range(n):
            out.append(self.mem[self.pointer])
            self.pointer = (self.pointer + 1) % self.size
        return bytes(out)


class MockTransport(Transport):
    def __init__(self, firmware: int = 0x09, mode: int = 0x40, serial: str = "00000001"):
        self.firmware = firmware
        self.mode = mode
        self.serial = serial
        self.unhandled: list[bytes] = []
        self._rx = bytearray()
        self._tx = bytearray()
        self.closed = False
        self._force_nack: int | None = None
        # ASSUMPTION: power-up IO_TYPE is all digital input. Changelog v7 (p.2) says only
        # I/O1 and I/O2 power up as inputs; I/O3 and I/O4 are assumed the same.
        self.io_type = 0xAA
        self.inputs = 0  # test-settable: 4-bit levels seen on digital-input pins
        self.adc = [0, 0, 0, 0]  # test-settable: raw 0-1023 per channel
        self._out = 0  # output levels, bit n = I/O(n+1)
        self._apply_io_type(self.io_type)
        self._force_setpins_nack = False
        self.serial_sent = bytearray()
        self.hold_serial_tx = False  # test-only: keep accepted bytes pending
        self._tx_pending = bytearray()
        self._serial_rx = bytearray()
        self.i2c_devices: dict[int, MockI2cDevice] = {}  # keyed by even 8-bit address; empty like the bench bus

    def _is_i2c_mode(self) -> bool:
        return self.mode in iss.I2C_MODES or bool(self.mode & iss.SERIAL and self.mode & ~iss.SERIAL in iss.I2C_MODES)

    def force_next_setpins_nack(self) -> None:
        """Test-only: the next SETPINS is consumed and answered 00."""

content.content:
SPI Mode
In SPI mode the USB-ISS is always the master and supplies the SCK signal, and always returns the same number of
bytes as you send.
The format is simple:

Send          SPI command       TxData1     TxData2       TxData3   …       TxData n
              (0x61)
Receive       Ack (0xFF) or     RxData1     RxData2       RxData3   ..      RxData n
              Nack (0x00)


All bytes should be sent to the USB-ISS in one sequence. A gap will result in the USB-ISS re-starting its internal
command synchronization loop and ignoring the message. The maximum frame length including the command is 63
bytes.
Here is an example of using SPI mode to communicate with Microchip's SPI SRAM, the 23k256.
Make sure you have the power link removed so you are working at 3.3v, as the 23k256 does not work at 5v.
The power up default of the 23k256 is byte mode. Here we will change this to sequential mode so any number of bytes
can be read/written in the same frame. To do that we write to the status register. The command is:

Send          SPI command      0x01         0x41
              (0x61)
Receive       Ack (0xFF) or    0xnn         0xnn
              Nack (0x00)


This is a 3 byte command. The 0x01 is the 23k256's "write status register" command. 0x41 is the new status register
value. It puts the device into sequential mode and disables the hold.
You must read back the same number of bytes as you send, in this case three. Only the first byte contains useful
information. 0xnn are "don't care" bytes.
Next we will write four bytes to the SRAM.

Send        SPI command        0x02      0x00      0x00    0x12     0x34    0x56    0x78
            (0x61)
Receive     ACK (0xFF) or      0xnn      0xnn      0xnn    0xnn     0xnn    0xnn    0xnn
            NACK (0x00)




© Devantech Ltd 23/3/2026                 USB-ISS Documentation                                             17/23
 Here we follow the SPI command with 0x02 which is the 23k256's write command. The next two 0x00's are the address
high and address low of the SRAM address. These are followed by the four data bytes, in this case 0x12, 0x34, 0x56,
0x78.
To read back the same bytes you would do this:

Send        SPI command       0x03     0x00      0x00   0xnn    0xnn    0xnn    0xnn
            (0x61)
Receive     ACK (0xFF) or     0xnn     0xnn      0xnn   0x12    0x34    0x56    0x78
            NACK (0x00)

The 0x03 is the 23k256's read command followed by the address (0x0000). We can then send any four bytes
to clock the data out of the SRAM.




© Devantech Ltd 23/3/2026                USB-ISS Documentation                                         18/23
 =====P9-10
Setting I2C_MODE
There are 7 I2C commands as detailed above. They differ only in the SCL frequency and whether they use a software
bit bashed driver or the I2C hardware in the PIC chip. The I2C command on its own will have I/O on pins I/O1 and
I/O2.
This is a 4 byte setup command:

                     USB-ISS        ISS_MODE       I2C_MODE       IO_TYPE
       Send          0x5A           0x02           0x60           0x04
       Receive       0xFF           0x00

This example will initialize I2C to 100khz using the hardware I2C peripheral in the PIC chip.

Setting I2C_MODE + SERIAL
The I2C commands may be combined with SERIAL mode. When combined with SERIAL, I/O1 is the Rx
pin and I/O2 is the Tx pin.

This is a 5 byte setup command:


                     USB-ISS       ISS_MODE       I2C_MODE+ Baud rate         Baud rate
                                                  SERIAL    (high byte)       (low byte)
       Send          0x5A          0x02           0x61           0x00         0x9B
       Receive       0xFF          0x00

The formula for calculating the baud rate is the same as for I/O+Serial above.




© Devantech Ltd 23/3/2026                 USB-ISS Documentation                                          9/23
 Setting SPI_MODE
This mode requires all four I/O pins, so cannot be combined with serial, I2C or I/O. Refer to the connection diagram for
pin-outs. SPI mode is capable of operating in all four possible clock phases.
SPI_MODE command (0x90) may combined with the phase selection bits.

SPI_MODE           Phase
0x90               Tx on transition from active to Idle clock, Idle state for clock is low level
0x91               Tx on transition from active to Idle clock, Idle state for clock is high level
0x92               Tx on transition from Idle to active clock, Idle state for clock is low level
0x93               Tx on transition from Idle to active clock, Idle state for clock is high level


0x90 is the standard mode, use this with SPI SRAM, EEPROM's etc.
Setting SPI mode is a 4 byte command:

                      USB-ISS        ISS_MODE         SPI_MODE         SCK divisor
       Send           0x5A           0x02             0x90             0x01
       Receive        0xFF           0x00

The SCK divisor sets the SPI clock speed. The formula is:

        Divisor = (6000000/SCK)-1

For a 3Mhz SCK:

        divisor = (6000000/3000000)-1 = 1

For 500khz SCK:

        divisor = (6000000/500000)-1 = 11

The maximum divisor of 255 gives the slowest SCK of just 23.44khz. A minimum of 0x01 should be set for
the divisor, if you set 0x00 it will be the same as 0x01.




© Devantech Ltd 23/3/2026                   USB-ISS Documentation                                          10/23
 ====P3
Pin descriptions
The below diagram shows the different pin functions for each USB-ISS mode.
             Power Link – Remove for 3.3v operation.            I/O         SPI        Serial      I2C        I2C +
                                                                                                              Serial
                                                                3.3v/5v     3.3v/5v    3.3v/5v     3.3v/5v    3.3v/5v
                                                                I/O4        SDI        I/O4        SDA        SDA
                                                                I/O3        SCK        I/O3        SCL        SCL
                                                                I/O2        SDO        TX          I/O2       TX
                                                                I/O1        CE         RX          I/O1       RX
                                                                GND         GND        GND         GND        GND


       Bootloader Link – Fit link for bootloader mode.


3.3v or 5v
There is a link beside the USB port for selecting between 5v, 3.3v operation.
The processor on the USB-ISS is equally happy running from 3.3v or from 5v. With the LEDs it takes up to 20mA, so
when 5v is selected by linking the power select pins the USB-ISS module can supply up to 80mA to external devices.
When the link is removed a 3.3v regulator supplies the power. This regulator is capable of 50mA, so when running at
3.3v up to 30mA is available to your circuits.
If your application requires more than this, or has its own supply, then leave the 3.3v/5v pin unconnected. Do not apply
your own voltage to this pin.

I/O pins
Each I/O pin, 1 to 4, may be individually selected to be Analogue Input or Digital Input or Digital Output. Inputs will
not accept voltage higher than the supply, so when operating at 3.3v the inputs are not 5v tolerant.
Analogue inputs span from 0v to the supply for a range of 0-1023 (10-bit A/D conversion).

SCL and SDA
These pins are the I2C bus connections and should be connected to the SCL and SDA pins on your I2C device. The
USB-ISS module is always a bus master, and is fitted with 4.7k pull-up resistors on the PCB. These resistors are
automatically disconnected in other modes.

SDI, SDO, SCK and CE
SDI is the SPI input to the USB-ISS, connect it to SDO on your device.
SDO is the SPI output from the USB-ISS, connect it to SDI on your device.
SCK is the SPI clock output from the USB-ISS, connect it to SCK on your device.
CE is the active low chip enable signal, connect it to CE on your device.

TX and RX
These are logic level signals, not RS232. Do not connect this to an RS232 port without using a suitable RS232 logic
level inverter chip.


© Devantech Ltd 23/3/2026                  USB-ISS Documentation                                              3/23

Communication
Plugging the module to Windows 10, Linux or MAC OS X will result in the module automatically presenting itself as a
virtual com port. The commands from the table further down can then be easily sent as if you were talking to a serial
port. Please note there is no need to set the baud rate as it has no effect.

Which COM/ Serial port?
After plugging in the USB-OPTO-RLY88 to a spare USB port, you will want to know which port it has been assigned
to. This will vary from system to system.

    Windows:
    Right click on the Start icon in your task bar and select "Device Manager". Now scroll down and open the "Ports
    (COM & LPT)" tab. You should see the USB serial port listed - COM4 in the example below.




    Linux
    To see a list of the available devices open a terminal window and run the following command:
      ls /dev/serial/by-id/

    Mac OS
    To see a list of the available devices open a terminal window and run the following command:
      ls /dev/cu.*
